transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today?

Well, thank you for seeing me, doctor. I, uh... I came in today because things have just gotten completely out of hand, and I really didn't know where else to turn. It’s... it’s about flying. Airplanes, specifically. I came because the thought—honestly, just the very thought of getting on an airplane now scares me so bad. 

And the most frustrating part of all of this, the thing that really drives me absolutely crazy, is that I know it does not make sense. I’m a logical person, I know the statistics, I know how safe commercial travel is supposed to be compared to driving a car or anything else. I try to tell myself all the facts. But none of that logic matters at all when it actually comes down to it. It’s like there’s a complete disconnect between my brain and my physical reactions, because my body just takes over entirely. My body tells me, with this absolute, terrifying certainty, that the plane is going to fall. It just screams at me that if I step foot on that aircraft, it is going to drop right out of the sky. I try to reason with myself, I really do, but that intense physical dread is just so overwhelming that I can't talk myself out of it.
Has this fear of flying been happening in other situations as well, or does it only occur specifically when you think about or are near airplanes?

Well, it's... it's definitely tied directly to airplanes, but it doesn't just happen when I'm at the airport or actually looking at a plane. It's the whole... the whole concept of it, really. You see, as a physician, I occasionally get asked to cover these rural shifts, and they require a short flight to get there. And I'm telling you, doctor, even if I'm just sitting in my living room, completely safe, and I just get an email—just a simple, routine email—asking if I can take one of those shifts... the reaction is immediate. 

I mean, the second I read the word "flight" or "fly" in the message, my heart just starts pounding out of my chest. It's like it's trying to break my ribs. And my hands get completely drenched in sweat, just instantly clammy and shaking. I literally feel like I cannot pull a full breath of air into my lungs. I start gasping, almost like I'm suffocating right there at my desk. And this intense, horrible feeling doesn't stop, it doesn't even begin to dial back, until I physically close the message or delete the email and try to completely block it out of my mind. So, it's not just being near them. It's... it's the anticipation, the mere suggestion that I might have to get on one. That alone is enough to send my body into absolute overdrive.
Have you ever experienced these kinds of physical reactions—like a pounding heart, sweating, shaking, or trouble breathing—when you weren't thinking about flying?

No, no, never. I mean, I've really thought about this, because as a doctor myself, you try to self-diagnose, right? You try to look at the whole clinical picture. But I can say with absolute certainty that these reactions—the heart racing like a freight train, the sweating where I'm just dripping onto my keyboard, that awful, suffocating feeling where I'm gasping for air—none of that has ever happened in any other context. 

It's not like I'm just an anxious person in general. I handle stress at the hospital all the time. I can manage a code blue, I can deal with difficult patients, I can work a 24-hour shift and keep my cool. I don't get panic attacks out of nowhere. I don't get nervous in elevators or tight spaces. I don't have issues with heights if I'm, say, looking out the window of a tall building. It is entirely, 100 percent, exclusively tied to airplanes and flying. If I'm not thinking about a flight, if I'm not being asked to take a flight, my body is perfectly fine. My heart rate is normal, my breathing is fine. It's just... it's just this one very specific, very localized trigger that just completely short-circuits my entire system. So, no, to answer your question, it never happens out of the blue or with anything else. Only flying.
